en: Rest areas on a motorway with fuel, food, and toilets.
High-speed roads with controlled access for most traffic, shown by blue signs in the UK.
To start moving from a stopped position, such as pulling away from the kerb or after waiting.
Starting to drive away after you have been stationary.
A bridge where the road is too narrow for two vehicles to pass easily side by side.
The road becoming less wide ahead.
The default UK speed limit when no numbered limit signs are shown (varies by road type and vehicle).
Damage to the neck bones, muscles, or spinal cord that can be serious after a crash.
A gear position where the engine is not connected to the wheels.
The downward weight a trailer’s hitch puts on the vehicle’s tow ball; it must stay within limits.
The plate on a vehicle that shows its registration number.
Partly hidden or hard to see, for example by dirt, trees, or another object.
Something blocking the road so traffic cannot pass freely.
Blocks or gets in the way of other traffic so it cannot pass freely.
Eight-sided shape; in the UK the STOP sign is octagonal.
Vehicles travelling toward you from the opposite direction.
A street where traffic is allowed to travel in only one direction.
A street where traffic is allowed to travel in only one direction.
Lights above each lane that show whether that lane is open or closed to traffic.
Carrying more weight than the vehicle or trailer is legally allowed to carry.
Pass a person riding a horse on the road; horses can be startled by noise and speed.
When another vehicle has passed you and moved ahead of you.
Passing a slower vehicle by moving alongside and ahead of it.
Vehicles that are passing you or about to pass you.
The brake (often a handbrake) that holds the vehicle still when parked.
Dim sidelights left on when parked so others can see your vehicle at night.
Rules that limit where and when you may park, shown by signs or road markings.
A widened section of a narrow road where vehicles can pass or wait.
Widened spots on a narrow road where vehicles can pull in to let others pass.
The raised path beside the road for people walking (sidewalk).
The busiest times of day when roads are most congested (rush hour).
Busy periods when many people travel, often morning and evening rush hours.
A marked place on the road where people on foot can cross safely.
Areas where motor vehicles are normally not allowed and only people on foot may use the space.
A pedestrian crossing controlled by traffic lights, including a flashing amber phase.
Points added to your driving licence after certain traffic offences.
Small electric vehicles for people with limited mobility, usually for pavements and short trips.
A major UK road between towns and cities, usually signed in green with white lettering.
The right to go first when roads meet or when rules give you precedence.
A rule that forbids a particular action or type of vehicle.
A learner driving licence that allows practice driving under set restrictions before a full licence.
When a vehicle starts moving off from a stop, such as leaving a bus stop.
Move to the side of the road and stop safely.
The vehicle steers or veers left or right by itself when you brake or drive.
A flat tyre caused by a hole that lets the air out.
Pedestrian traffic lights started by pressing a button at the crossing.
A line of vehicles waiting or moving slowly.
Lines of slow-moving or waiting traffic.
A place where a road crosses railway tracks, often with lights, barriers, or alarms.
Bright red lights at the back of a vehicle used only in thick fog to help others see you.
A child seat that faces backwards, safer for infants in a crash.
A side-lying first-aid position that helps keep an unconscious breathing person’s airway clear.
A road marked with red lines where stopping and parking are tightly controlled.
UK roads marked with red lines where stopping and parking are tightly restricted.
Clothes that shine when light hits them, helping others see the wearer.
Bright reflective strips or panels that help others see a vehicle, especially in the dark.
Cat’s-eye markers set in the road that reflect light to show lane edges at night.
A bright yellow sign that warns drivers they are near a school.
A safe lay-by beside a motorway where you can stop if you have a problem.
The person named on the vehicle registration as responsible for the vehicle records.
The V5C paper that records the vehicle’s details and its registered keeper.
A neighbourhood of homes where traffic and pedestrians are often close together.
Roads in housing areas where people live, often with parked cars and pedestrians.
A safety device that holds a child securely in the vehicle, such as a child seat.
Straps, ropes, or other fittings used to hold a load firmly in place.
A limit on what you may do, such as speed, access, or vehicle type.
Driving the vehicle backwards.
